title: Utility types
subtitle: Partial, Pick/Omit, union tools, ReturnType, Nest DTO derivation

cards.front: Why do utility types exist?
cards.meaning: They are built-in generic types that transform other types so you keep a single source of truth (entity/DTO) and derive variants instead of duplicating 15 fields by hand. Add a field to User and derived DTOs pick it up unless you omitted it.

cards.front: What are utility types under the hood?
cards.meaning: Mostly mapped and conditional types (advanced chapter). This unit is fluent use and Nest-style DTO derivation; knowing the sketches explains why they compose with keyof and unions.

cards.front: What does Partial<T> do, and typical use?
cards.meaning: Makes all properties optional. Typical use: PATCH bodies and partial forms.
cards.example: type UserPatch = Partial<User>; // { id?: string; name?: string }

cards.front: Is Partial<T> deep?
cards.meaning: No — it is shallow. Nested objects are not deeply optional. A deep partial needs a custom mapped type (advanced).

cards.front: What does Required<T> do, and typical use?
cards.meaning: Makes all properties required. Typical use: a fully filled config object.
cards.example: type Full = Required<{ a?: string; b?: number }>; // { a: string; b: number }

cards.front: What does Readonly<T> do, and typical use?
cards.meaning: Makes all properties readonly. Typical use: immutable state shapes. Prevents reassignment of properties on that type.
cards.example: type ImmutableUser = Readonly<User>; // readonly id, readonly name

cards.front: Does Readonly<T> freeze values at runtime?
cards.meaning: No. It is shallow and compile-time only — not deep immutability at runtime (still erasure). It is not Object.freeze.

cards.front: What does Pick<T, K> do, and typical use?
cards.meaning: Keeps only keys K. Typical use: a form subset of a DTO. K must be (or extend) keyof T.

cards.front: What does Omit<T, K> do, and typical use?
cards.meaning: Drops keys K. Typical use: strip id / secrets. It is the practical “everything except…” transformer.

cards.front: Pick vs Omit — when which?
cards.meaning: Prefer Omit for “entity minus server fields”; prefer Pick when the allowlist is short and explicit. K for Pick must extend keyof T.

cards.front: What does Record<K, V> do, and typical use?
cards.meaning: An object type with keys K and values V. Typical use: dictionaries / maps — Record<string, User> or Record<'loading' | 'success' | 'error', string>.

cards.front: Why Record of a literal union vs Record<string, V>?
cards.meaning: When K is a literal union, keys become a required property set — good for exhaustive maps (pair with satisfies/Record and discriminant unions). Record<string, V> allows any string key and is weaker.

cards.front: What does Exclude<T, U> do, and typical use?
cards.meaning: Union minus members assignable to U (distributes over members). Typical use: strip a variant.

cards.front: What does Extract<T, U> do, and typical use?
cards.meaning: Union keeping members assignable to U. Typical use: pull a variant. Also used on object unions: Extract<Event, { type: 'click' }>.

cards.front: Exclude vs Omit — which works on what?
cards.meaning: Exclude filters unions (distributive). Omit drops object keys (often thought of as Pick plus Exclude on keyof T). Do not confuse union filtering with key dropping.

cards.front: What does NonNullable<T> do?
cards.meaning: Removes null | undefined from T. Typical use: after a guard, or when modeling a required value. Equivalent idea: Exclude<T, null | undefined>.
cards.example: type U = NonNullable<string | null | undefined>; // string

cards.front: What does ReturnType<F> do, and typical use?
cards.meaning: The return type of function type F. Typical use: derive from an existing function instead of duplicating the return interface by hand. F must be a function type, often typeof someFn.

cards.front: What does Parameters<F> do, and typical use?
cards.meaning: The parameter tuple of function type F. Typical use: wrappers and proxies so argument types do not drift from the wrapped function.

cards.front: What is the ReturnType trap on overloads?
cards.meaning: ReturnType on an overloaded function may pick an unexpected overload signature. Do not assume it always matches the overload you call at runtime.

cards.front: What does Awaited<T> do, and typical use?
cards.meaning: Unwraps Promise, including nested promises. Typical use: the resolved type of an async function, often composed as Awaited<ReturnType<typeof fn>>.
cards.example: type User = Awaited<Promise<Promise<{ id: string }>>>; // { id: string }

cards.front: How do you type the resolved value of fetchUser?
cards.meaning: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof fetchUser>>. ReturnType of an async function is Promise<…>; Awaited unwraps to the inner value so you do not duplicate the User shape.

cards.front: How do you derive a public User response DTO?
cards.meaning: Omit secrets: type UserResponseDto = Omit<User, 'passwordHash'>. Public response is Omit<Entity, SecretKeys> or a short Pick allowlist.

cards.front: How do you derive CreateUserDto from User?
cards.meaning: Omit server keys, then & add client-only fields: Omit<User, 'id' | 'createdAt' | 'passwordHash'> & { password: string }. Compose with & when you need to add fields after omitting secrets.

cards.front: How do you derive UpdateUserDto / PATCH from User?
cards.meaning: Partial<Omit<User, 'id' | 'createdAt' | 'passwordHash'>> — Omit removes non-client-settable fields; Partial makes the rest optional for PATCH. New User fields flow into the DTO automatically.

cards.front: Why & after Omit when replacing passwordHash?
cards.meaning: Omit drops passwordHash; & { password: string } adds the create-body field. Forgetting & after Omit is a common mistake when replacement fields are needed.

cards.front: Can you call Partial(user) at runtime?
cards.meaning: No. Utilities are types only and erased. There is no Partial() runtime function from TypeScript. Nest still needs class-validator or Zod for runtime validation — same erasure story.

cards.front: Composition cheat: PATCH body?
cards.meaning: Partial<Omit<Entity, LockedKeys>>. Order for readability: usually Omit/Pick first, then Partial/Readonly, then & additions.

cards.front: Composition cheat: public response?
cards.meaning: Omit<Entity, SecretKeys> or Pick when the allowlist is short and explicit.

cards.front: Composition cheat: create body?
cards.meaning: Omit<Entity, ServerKeys> & { password: string } (or other client-only fields).

cards.front: Does utility composition order matter?
cards.meaning: For readability, usually Omit/Pick first, then Partial/Readonly, then & additions. That matches PATCH (Partial of an Omit) and create (Omit then &).

cards.front: Sketch of Partial — do you need the full definition?
cards.meaning: type Partial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }. Sketch only — do not memorize full definitions yet. It explains composition with keyof.
cards.example: type Partial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] };

cards.front: Sketch of Pick?
cards.meaning: type Pick<T, K extends keyof T> = { [P in K]: T[P] }. Mapped over the chosen keys; K is constrained to keyof T.
cards.example: type Pick<T, K extends keyof T> = { [P in K]: T[P] };

cards.front: Sketch of Exclude?
cards.meaning: type Exclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T. Conditional type that distributes over union members — the bridge to the conditional-types chapter.
cards.example: type Exclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T;

cards.front: Partial vs handwriting every field optional?
cards.meaning: Partial derives optionality from the entity so new fields flow in. Hand-writing optional bags duplicates fields and drifts when the entity changes — utilities exist to avoid that.

cards.front: Why not duplicate DTOs by hand because utilities feel scary?
cards.meaning: You lose the single-source-of-truth benefit. Prefer composing Partial/Omit/Pick/& from one entity; utilities are the fluent layer over mapped/conditional types.
